title: antichamber
text: This game is not like any other pzzle game out there. The puzzle games we know and love is more or less, put block here and it will open a door there. This game takes that and throws it out a 100 floor building, then proceeds to jump with it. The people behind this game really naild it with the puzzle aspect as well as to blow the mind of the player. Countless times i was amazed by the simple complexity of some of the puzzles you incounter. For example Imagine you’re walking down a series of hallways, one after another. Every turn you take only results in another hallway. You don’t even know where you’re going, but you do know that you don’t want to be there anymore. In an act of desperation, you turn around. Suddenly, the area behind you is completely new. It is most certainly not where you came from, but it is where you are going now. Around each corner in Antichamber awaits a complete mystery; you never know what you’re going to get. Even when viewing something, it is hard to be certain what is there and what isn’t. It's because the game succeeds in using non-Euclidean geometry, or a set of geometric rules that aren't consistent in logic. After each puzzle there are brief hints accompanied by a picture. The starting area contains a map of all the rooms and how they connect, each room revealed only as it is encountered. This main lobby area can be accessed at any time by pressing the Esc key. This becomes useful in a handful of situations, since it shows the room you were last in. It also allows you to teleport to any previously visited area, without traversing the maze and puzzles again. Dont let me get started on the gun you get, that can remove or place blocks at will. All and all this game is amazing and should be checked out. 10/10 in my book.

title: antichamber
text: I don't do many puzzle games, but I definitely enjoyed this one. It challenges you to think differently - spatially, laterally, logically, etc. This game is most definitely NOT a lateral storyline game - you'll be all over the map, usually because the end of one puzzle/level 'jumps' (teleports) to a completely different part of the map.  Sometimes the trickery can feel a bit gratuitous(?), but overall as you progress through the game you should naturally pick up the knowledge you need to succeed. I finished the game in about 15hrs of play, and I might have done it a bit more quickly if I wasn't absolutely hung on a puzzle for quite some time. So the $20 price may be a bit steep for that amount of one-run game play, but I bet it has good replayability - let it sit for 6 months and you'll probably forget 90% of the stuff and have to learn it over again! And if you can get it on a Steam sale, it's absolutely worth it at a discounted price!

text: Arma II is a commendable game on many levels.  It is open, it tries to be realistic, and in many ways it succeeds.  There are plausible scenarios, tons of weapons, interesting views and tactics.  But.  The UI is clunky, the controls are clunky the feel of the game itself is clunky and needlessly complex.  On top of these points, the dialogue and music are hardly compelling, in fact, they are like cheese on a soggy pizza.  Yes, it's technically pizza, and pizza is good, but this is some bad cheese. The best part about Arma II is that you can mod Arma II.  You can add extra toppings to make the whole thing a little more palatable.  Can I recommend Arma II as a buy that is used to create a fun gaming experience?  Absolutely.  Can I recommend it as a stand-alone product?  Unlikely.  This review reflects Arma II as a standalone game, and as a standalone piece of software it gets a 6.8/10.  Mediocre at best despite its grand aspirations.
